claim: Larval zebrafish initiate hunting by rapidly converging their eyes, which substantially increases their binocular visual field.
source: A defining characteristic is that larvae initiate hunting by rapidly converging their eyes, which substantially increases their binocular visual field (Bianco et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianco et al., 2011

claim: A high vergence angle is maintained during prey pursuit in larval zebrafish.
source: A high vergence angle is maintained during prey pursuit, which entails a sequence of discrete orienting turns and approach swims, which culminate in binocular fixation of prey followed by a kinematically distinct capture swim (Borla et al., 2002; McElligott and O'malley, 2005; Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Prey pursuit in larval zebrafish entails a sequence of discrete orienting turns and approach swims.
source: A high vergence angle is maintained during prey pursuit, which entails a sequence of discrete orienting turns and approach swims, which culminate in binocular fixation of prey followed by a kinematically distinct capture swim (Borla et al., 2002; McElligott and O'malley, 2005; Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Prey pursuit in larval zebrafish culminates in binocular fixation of prey followed by a kinematically distinct capture swim.
source: A high vergence angle is maintained during prey pursuit, which entails a sequence of discrete orienting turns and approach swims, which culminate in binocular fixation of prey followed by a kinematically distinct capture swim (Borla et al., 2002; McElligott and O'malley, 2005; Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Neural activity associated with prey-like visual cues has been detected in the axon terminals of a specific class of retinal ganglion cell (RGC), which terminate in retinal arborisation field 7 (AF7) in the pretectum.
source: Neural activity associated with prey-like visual cues has been detected in the axon terminals of a specific class of retinal ganglion cell (RGC), which terminate in retinal arborisation field 7 (AF7) in the pretectum (Semmelhack et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Semmelhack et al., 2014

claim: Prey-responsive pretectal cells have been described in larval zebrafish.
source: Prey-responsive pretectal cells have also been described (Muto et al., 2017) as well as highly prey-selective feature-analysing neurons in the optic tectum (OT) that display non-linear mixed selectivity for conjunctions of visual features (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muto et al., 2017

claim: Highly prey-selective feature-analysing neurons in the optic tectum display non-linear mixed selectivity for conjunctions of visual features.
source: Prey-responsive pretectal cells have also been described (Muto et al., 2017) as well as highly prey-selective feature-analysing neurons in the optic tectum (OT) that display non-linear mixed selectivity for conjunctions of visual features (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianco and Engert, 2015

claim: Premotor activity in localised tectal assemblies immediately precedes execution of hunting responses.
source: Premotor activity in localised tectal assemblies immediately precedes execution of hunting responses (Bianco and Engert, 2015) and optogenetic stimulation of the anterior-ventral tectal region can induce hunting-like behaviour (Fajardo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianco and Engert, 2015

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the anterior-ventral tectal region can induce hunting-like behaviour.
source: Premotor activity in localised tectal assemblies immediately precedes execution of hunting responses (Bianco and Engert, 2015) and optogenetic stimulation of the anterior-ventral tectal region can induce hunting-like behaviour (Fajardo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fajardo et al., 2013

claim: Ablation of RGC input to AF7 substantially impairs hunting in larval zebrafish.
source: Finally, ablation of RGC input to either AF7 or OT substantially impairs hunting (Gahtan et al., 2005; Semmelhack et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gahtan et al., 2005 and Semmelhack et al., 2014

claim: Ablation of RGC input to OT substantially impairs hunting in larval zebrafish.
source: Finally, ablation of RGC input to either AF7 or OT substantially impairs hunting (Gahtan et al., 2005; Semmelhack et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gahtan et al., 2005 and Semmelhack et al., 2014

claim: 2-photon calcium imaging was performed in transgenic elavl3:H2B-GCaMP6s;atoh7:gapRFP larvae (6–7 dpf, N = 8) during a virtual hunting assay.
source: Transgenic elavl3:H2B-GCaMP6s;atoh7:gapRFP larvae (6–7 dpf, N = 8) were partially restrained in agarose gel, but with their eyes and tail free to move, and were presented with a range of visual cues including small moving prey-like spots, which evoke naturalistic hunting responses (Figure 1B) (Bianco et al., 2011; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Experimental procedure described in methods

claim: The imaging volume encompassed the majority of the primary retinorecipient sites (arborisation fields 2–10) as well as surrounding brain regions including pretectum and OT (310 × 310 × 100 µm volume).
source: We imaged a volume that encompassed the majority of the primary retinorecipient sites [arborisation fields (AFs) 2–10] as well as surrounding brain regions including pretectum and OT (310 × 310 × 100 µm volume; Figure 1C and Video 1).
evidence: Experimental procedure described with reference to Figure 1C

claim: 91.6 ± 4.9% of convergent saccades were paired with tail movement.
source: These are defined by saccadic convergence of the eyes – an oculomotor behaviour specific to hunting initiation and frequently coincident with lateralised tail movements (91.6 ± 4.9% of convergent saccades paired with tail movement; eye-tail latency 11.6 ± 5.2 ms, mean ± SD; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) (Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: Eye-tail latency during hunting initiation is 11.6 ± 5.2 ms (mean ± SD).
source: These are defined by saccadic convergence of the eyes – an oculomotor behaviour specific to hunting initiation and frequently coincident with lateralised tail movements (91.6 ± 4.9% of convergent saccades paired with tail movement; eye-tail latency 11.6 ± 5.2 ms, mean ± SD; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) (Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: Larvae preferentially responded to small, dark, moving spots.
source: Larvae preferentially responded to small, dark, moving spots and hunting was initiated most frequently once the stimulus had crossed the midline axis and was moving in a nose-tail direction (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figures

claim: Hunting was initiated most frequently once the stimulus had crossed the midline axis and was moving in a nose-tail direction.
source: Larvae preferentially responded to small, dark, moving spots and hunting was initiated most frequently once the stimulus had crossed the midline axis and was moving in a nose-tail direction (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figures and citation

claim: Unsupervised clustering classified more than 50% of imaged neurons (93,054 out of 181,123 cells) into 36 clusters with homogenous functional properties.
source: This approach allowed us to classify more than 50% of imaged neurons (93,054 out of 181,123 cells) into 36 clusters with homogenous functional properties (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Result of computational analysis on experimental data

claim: Four clusters (clusters 25–28) showed activity highly correlated with eye convergence events.
source: Specifically, four clusters showed activity highly correlated with eye convergence events (clusters 25–28; Figure 1I) yet exhibited little activity in response to visual cues (including prey-like moving spots; Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis with reference to figures

claim: Clusters 25–28 exhibited little activity in response to visual cues including prey-like moving spots.
source: Specifically, four clusters showed activity highly correlated with eye convergence events (clusters 25–28; Figure 1I) yet exhibited little activity in response to visual cues (including prey-like moving spots; Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis with reference to figures

claim: Cluster 26 was selective for convergent saccades associated with leftwards turns.
source: In two of these clusters, activity was selective for the direction of motor responses. Thus, cluster 26 was selective for convergent saccades associated with leftwards turns and cluster 28 was tuned to rightwards hunting responses.
evidence: Result of functional analysis

claim: Cluster 28 was tuned to rightwards hunting responses.
source: In two of these clusters, activity was selective for the direction of motor responses. Thus, cluster 26 was selective for convergent saccades associated with leftwards turns and cluster 28 was tuned to rightwards hunting responses.
evidence: Result of functional analysis

claim: Cluster 25 was associated with convergent saccades paired with symmetrical/no tail movement.
source: By contrast, the other two clusters did not show selectivity for the direction of tail movements during hunting initiation (cluster 25, associated with symmetrical/no tail movement and 27, responsive to motion in either direction).
evidence: Result of functional analysis

claim: Cluster 27 was responsive to motion in either direction during hunting initiation.
source: By contrast, the other two clusters did not show selectivity for the direction of tail movements during hunting initiation (cluster 25, associated with symmetrical/no tail movement and 27, responsive to motion in either direction).
evidence: Result of functional analysis

claim: Neurons in clusters 25–28 showed considerably higher HIx scores than other cells, including those in prey-responsive clusters.
source: This analysis revealed that neurons in clusters 25–28 showed considerably higher HIx scores than other cells, including those in prey-responsive clusters (1 and 4, Figure 1K).
evidence: Result of hunting index analysis with reference to Figure 1K

claim: A high density of neurons in hunting-initiation clusters were located in the pretectum in the immediate vicinity of AF7.
source: Notably, a high density of neurons belonging to hunting-initiation clusters were found in pretectal regions in the immediate vicinity of AF7 (AF7-pretectum), just anterior to the rostral pole of the optic tectum (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Result of anatomical registration analysis with reference to figures

claim: Neurons selective for the direction of hunting-related tail motion (clusters 26 and 28) showed lateralised, mirror-symmetric distributions.
source: Neurons selective for the direction of hunting-related tail motion (clusters 26 and 28) showed lateralised, mirror-symmetric distributions, with a larger fraction of cells located on the side of the brain contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis with reference to Figure 2A

claim: A larger fraction of direction-selective hunting neurons were located on the side of the brain contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement.
source: Neurons selective for the direction of hunting-related tail motion (clusters 26 and 28) showed lateralised, mirror-symmetric distributions, with a larger fraction of cells located on the side of the brain contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis with reference to Figure 2A

claim: Cluster 26, which is tuned to eye convergence associated with leftwards tail movement, had a higher density of cells in the right AF7-pretectum.
source: Specifically, cluster 26, which is tuned to eye convergence associated with leftwards tail movement, had a higher density of cells in the right AF7-pretectum, and vice versa for cluster 28.
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis

claim: Hunting-initiation clusters that were agnostic to tail direction (clusters 25 and 27) showed largely symmetric anatomical distributions.
source: Hunting-initiation clusters that were agnostic to tail direction (clusters 25 and 27) showed largely symmetric anatomical distributions (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis with reference to Figure 2A

claim: Prey-responsive neurons were found in AF7-pretectum as well as in the medial thalamus.
source: Neurons belonging to prey-responsive clusters were also found in AF7-pretectum as well as in the medial thalamus, where direction-selective neurons showed highly lateralised distributions (Figure 2A,B, left panel).
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis with reference to figures

claim: Direction-selective prey-responsive neurons in the medial thalamus showed highly lateralised distributions.
source: Neurons belonging to prey-responsive clusters were also found in AF7-pretectum as well as in the medial thalamus, where direction-selective neurons showed highly lateralised distributions (Figure 2A,B, left panel).
evidence: Result of anatomical analysis with reference to figures

claim: Prey-responsive neurons in clusters 1 and 4 showed direction-selective activity in response to small dark moving spots, but minimal activity associated with convergent saccades.
source: This confirmed that prey-responsive neurons in clusters 1 and 4 showed direction-selective activity in response to small dark moving spots, but minimal activity associated with convergent saccades (Figure 2C,D, left columns).
evidence: Result of functional analysis with reference to figures

claim: Hunting-initiation neurons (clusters 25–28) showed weak visual responses during non-response trials but substantial activity triggered on hunting initiation.
source: In contrast, hunting-initiation neurons (clusters 25–28) showed weak visual responses – as shown by moving spot-triggered activity during non-response trials – but substantial activity triggered on hunting initiation.
evidence: Result of functional analysis

claim: For clusters 26 and 28, neurons showed stronger activation when convergent saccades were paired with contraversive left and right-sided turns, respectively.
source: For clusters 26 and 28, neurons showed stronger activation when convergent saccades were paired with contraversive left and right-sided turns, respectively (Figure 2C,D, right columns).
evidence: Result of functional analysis with reference to figures

claim: The KalTA4u508 transgene labels neurons in the AF7-pretectal region.
source: To characterise the connectivity and function of AF7-pretectal neurons with hunting-initiation activity, we inspected the expression patterns of a range of transgenic driver lines and identified a transgene, KalTA4u508, which labels neurons in the AF7-pretectal region (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figures

claim: KalTA4u508 labels populations of cells within the midbrain, hindbrain, sensory ganglia and spinal cord as well as non-neural tissues.
source: Additionally, KalTA4u508 labels populations of cells within the midbrain, hindbrain, sensory ganglia and spinal cord as well as non-neural tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figure

claim: Anatomical registration of KalTA4u508;UAS:mCherry volumetric data revealed a high density of labelled somata in AF7-pretectum, overlapping with the locations of hunting-initiation clusters.
source: However, anatomical registration of KalTA4u508;UAS:mCherry volumetric data to the reference atlas revealed a high density of labelled somata in AF7-pretectum, overlapping with the locations of hunting-initiation clusters (Figure 3A,B,I).
evidence: Result of anatomical registration analysis with reference to figures

claim: A subset of KalTA4u508-expressing neurons extend dendritic arbours that directly juxtapose RGC terminals in AF7.
source: We generated KalTA4u508;UAS:RFP;atoh7:GFP larvae to visualise GFP-labelled RGC axon terminals in AF7, and observed that a subset of KalTA4u508-expressing neurons extend dendritic arbours that directly juxtapose RGC terminals (N = 4 fish; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figures

claim: In adult (3 month old) KalTA4u508;UAS:GCaMP6f;atoh7:gapRFP fish, labelled neurons in the pretectum were very sparse and could be identified only in the accessory pretectal nucleus (APN; N = 8 somata from four fish).
source: In brain sections from adult (3 month old) KalTA4u508;UAS:GCaMP6f;atoh7:gapRFP fish, labelled neurons in the pretectum were very sparse and could be identified only in the accessory pretectal nucleus (APN; N = 8 somata from four fish; Figure 3E).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figure

claim: At least a subset of KalTA4u508-expressing neurons reside in a region of the larval AF7-pretectum corresponding to the adult APN.
source: This suggests that at least a subset of KalTA4u508-expressing neurons reside in a region of the larval AF7-pretectum corresponding to the adult APN.
evidence: Inference from adult expression data

claim: One class of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons projects to the ipsilateral optic tectum, elaborating axon terminal arbours preferentially in the most anterior-ventral aspect of OT (N = 4 cells from four fish).
source: One class projects to the ipsilateral optic tectum (Figure 3F), elaborating axon terminal arbours preferentially in the most anterior-ventral aspect of OT (N = 4 cells from four fish; Figure 3G).
evidence: Result of single-cell morphological tracing with reference to figures

claim: A second class of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons makes descending projections to the midbrain and hindbrain tegmentum, with axons decussating near the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (nMLF) and the oculomotor nucleus (nIII) before extending caudally into the contralateral ventral hindbrain (N = 5 cells from five fish).
source: The second class makes descending projections to the midbrain and hindbrain tegmentum. Axons decussate near the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (nMLF) and the oculomotor nucleus (nIII) before extending caudally into the contralateral ventral hindbrain. Axon collaterals could be observed bilaterally in the vicinity of nIII/nMLF and proximal to ventral reticulospinal neurons in the contralateral hindbrain (N = 5 cells from five fish; Figure 3H).
evidence: Result of single-cell morphological tracing with reference to figure

claim: The second class of KalTA4u508 projection neurons extended dendrites within a neuropil region that includes AF7.
source: This class of projection neuron extended dendrites within a neuropil region that includes AF7 (Figure 3H'), a feature not observed in the other two classes.
evidence: Result of single-cell morphological tracing with reference to figure

claim: A third class of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons was characterised by ipsilateral axonal projections to the medial region of the corpus cerebellum (N = 2 cells from two fish).
source: The third class was characterised by ipsilateral axonal projections to the medial region of the corpus cerebellum (N = 2 cells from two fish; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Result of single-cell morphological tracing with reference to figure

claim: The subset of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons projecting to contralateral hindbrain belong to the larval APN.
source: In combination with our adult expression data (Figure 3E), we conclude that the subset of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons projecting to contralateral hindbrain belong to the larval APN.
evidence: Inference from morphological and adult expression data

claim: KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons exhibited negligible activity in response to visual stimuli.
source: Notably, KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons exhibited negligible activity in response to visual stimuli (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Result of calcium imaging experiments with reference to figures

claim: Approximately 51% of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons were assigned cluster identities based on functional archetypes (correlation threshold = 0.7, N = 188 out of 369 cells).
source: Visuomotor vectors were generated for individual cells allowing ~51% to be assigned cluster identities based on the functional archetypes established previously using pan-neuronal imaging (correlation threshold = 0.7, N = 188 out of 369 cells).
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis

claim: 28% of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons with assigned functional identities were associated with hunting-initiation clusters (clusters 25–28; 52/188 cells).
source: Of the KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons assigned functional identities, 28% were associated with hunting-initiation clusters (clusters 25–28; 52/188 cells; Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis with reference to figures

claim: The remaining KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons were assigned to either conjugate eye movement clusters (57%) or tail movement clusters (15%).
source: The remaining neurons were assigned to either conjugate eye movement clusters (57%) or tail movement clusters (15%) and, in line with the absence of visual sensory responses, no cells were assigned to prey-responsive clusters.
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis

claim: No KalTA4u508 pretectal cells were assigned to prey-responsive clusters.
source: The remaining neurons were assigned to either conjugate eye movement clusters (57%) or tail movement clusters (15%) and, in line with the absence of visual sensory responses, no cells were assigned to prey-responsive clusters.
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis

claim: Most KalTA4u508 hunting-initiation neurons were associated with functional clusters 26 and 28, which show direction-selective activity.
source: Of the hunting-initiation neurons, most KalTA4u508 cells were associated with functional clusters 26 and 28, which show direction-selective activity (Figure 4B,E) and neurons in these two clusters were predominantly located contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement (73% and 80% contralateral for cluster identities 26 and 28, respectively).
evidence: Result of functional clustering analysis with reference to figures

claim: Neurons in clusters 26 and 28 were predominantly located contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement (73% and 80% contralateral for cluster identities 26 and 28, respectively).
source: Of the hunting-initiation neurons, most KalTA4u508 cells were associated with functional clusters 26 and 28, which show direction-selective activity (Figure 4B,E) and neurons in these two clusters were predominantly located contralateral to the direction of preferred tail movement (73% and 80% contralateral for cluster identities 26 and 28, respectively).
evidence: Result of functional and anatomical analysis

claim: KalTA4u508 cells assigned to hunting-initiation clusters had higher HIx scores than those assigned to other clusters.
source: KalTA4u508 cells assigned to hunting-initiation clusters had higher HIx scores than those assigned to other clusters (Figure 4C) supporting the hunting-response specificity of their activity.
evidence: Result of hunting index analysis with reference to figure

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of individual KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons could induce sustained, hunting-like behavioural routines.
source: Strikingly, we found that optogenetic stimulation of individual KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons could induce sustained, hunting-like behavioural routines.
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments

claim: Optogenetically induced hunting routines comprised a sequence of swim bouts that coincided with a sustained period of elevated ocular vergence.
source: As in naturalistic hunting, optogenetically induced hunting routines comprised a sequence of swim bouts that coincided with a sustained period of elevated ocular vergence (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: Optogenetically induced hunting sequences were initiated by a convergent saccade accompanied by a lateralised swim bout.
source: These sequences were initiated by a convergent saccade accompanied by a lateralised swim bout (Figure 5C) and in several cases terminated with a bout resembling a capture swim and paired with jaw opening (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: In several cases, optogenetically induced hunting sequences terminated with a bout resembling a capture swim and paired with jaw opening.
source: These sequences were initiated by a convergent saccade accompanied by a lateralised swim bout (Figure 5C) and in several cases terminated with a bout resembling a capture swim and paired with jaw opening (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: The fraction of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons that induced hunting (32%, 23 out of 70 cells) was similar to the proportion that were assigned to hunting-initiation clusters (28%).
source: The fraction of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons that induced hunting (32%, 23 out of 70 cells) was similar to the proportion that were assigned to hunting-initiation clusters (28%; Figure 4B).
evidence: Comparison of optogenetic and functional clustering results

claim: For responsive fish, 18.1% median response probability was observed in LED-On trials vs. 0% in LED-Off trials (p<0.0001, N = 23 fish).
source: For responsive fish, we observed 18.1% median response probability in LED-On trials vs. 0% in LED-Off trials (p<0.0001, N = 23 fish; Figure 5F).
evidence: Statistical analysis of optogenetic experimental data with reference to figure

claim: Control experiments demonstrated that opsin-negative animals do not produce hunting behaviours in response to blue light stimulation alone (0/16 animals).
source: Furthermore, control experiments demonstrated that opsin-negative animals do not produce hunting behaviours in response to blue light stimulation alone (0/16 animals; Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Result of control experiments with reference to figure

claim: The KalTA4u508 cells that could evoke hunting behaviour belonged to the projection classes that innervated the ipsilateral optic tectum (9/23 cells) or that belong to the presumptive APN and connect to the contralateral tegmentum (14/23 cells).
source: By examining single-cell morphology, we found that the KalTA4u508 cells that could evoke hunting behaviour belonged to the projection classes that innervated the ipsilateral optic tectum (9/23 cells, hereafter abbreviated 'ipsi-projecting') or that belong to the presumptive APN and connect to the contralateral tegmentum (14/23 cells, 'contra-projecting'; Figure 5G,H).
evidence: Result of morphological analysis of optogenetically responsive cells with reference to figures

claim: The duration of hunting sequences and vergence angles were equivalent between natural and optogenetically evoked behaviour.
source: The duration of hunting sequences, defined by the period of elevated ocular vergence, as well as vergence angles, were equivalent between natural and optogenetically evoked behaviour (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: Comparison of kinematic measurements with reference to figures

claim: In 100% of optogenetically-evoked hunting routines, a lateralised swim bout immediately followed saccadic convergence with short latency, comparable to natural hunting.
source: In 100% of optogenetically-evoked hunting routines, a lateralised swim bout immediately followed saccadic convergence with short latency, comparable to natural hunting (Figure 5K).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with reference to figure

claim: Natural hunting bouts and optogenetically induced hunting bouts showed high degree of kinematic similarity in bout asymmetry, fraction of curvature localised to distal tail segments, and low tail beat frequency.
source: This revealed a high degree of kinematic similarity between natural hunting bouts and optogenetically induced hunting bouts. In both cases, bouts comprised a highly lateralised sequence of half-beats ('bout asymmetry'; Figure 5L, see Materials and methods for details), a large fraction of curvature was localised to the distal segments of the tail (Figure 5M) and bouts displayed low tail beat frequency (Figure 5N).
evidence: Kinematic analysis with reference to figures

claim: All kinematic parameters of optogenetically induced hunting bouts were significantly different as compared to spontaneous swims.
source: Notably, all such parameters were significantly different as compared to spontaneous swims.
evidence: Statistical comparison of kinematic data

claim: Optogenetically induced hunting bouts showed a reduction in average vigour and theta-1 angles compared to bouts during Paramecia hunting.
source: Optogenetically induced hunting bouts showed a reduction in average vigour and theta-1 angles (maximum tail angle during the first half beat) compared to bouts during Paramecia hunting (Figure 5O,P).
evidence: Kinematic comparison with reference to figures

claim: The laterality of evoked hunting responses differed between ipsi-projecting and contra-projecting KalTA4u508 neurons.
source: However, the laterality of evoked hunting responses differed between the two projection classes (Figure 5R,S): Stimulation of ipsi-projecting KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons most frequently induced hunting in which the first swim bout was oriented in the ipsilateral direction (i.e. a left pretectal neuron evoked leftward turning). By contrast, contra-projecting neurons most frequently induced contralaterally directed hunting responses.
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments comparing projection classes with reference to figures

claim: Stimulation of ipsi-projecting KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons most frequently induced hunting in which the first swim bout was oriented in the ipsilateral direction.
source: Stimulation of ipsi-projecting KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons most frequently induced hunting in which the first swim bout was oriented in the ipsilateral direction (i.e. a left pretectal neuron evoked leftward turning).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments

claim: Contra-projecting neurons most frequently induced contralaterally directed hunting responses.
source: By contrast, contra-projecting neurons most frequently induced contralaterally directed hunting responses.
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments

claim: KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons that can induce predatory behaviour by optogenetic stimulation all belonged to hunting-initiation clusters (clusters 25–27) and had high HIx scores (N = 6 cells from six fish).
source: Visuomotor fingerprinting and cluster assignment of these neurons showed that they all belonged to hunting-initiation clusters (clusters 25–27) and had high HIx scores (N = 6 cells from six fish; Figure 5T).
evidence: Result of combined optogenetic and calcium imaging experiments with reference to figure

claim: Optogenetic activation of multiple KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons reliably evoked hunting behaviour at short latency.
source: Optogenetic activation of multiple KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons reliably evoked hunting behaviour at short latency.
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments

claim: Unilateral stimulation of the AF7-pretectal population induced convergent saccades paired with lateralised tail movements with high response probability (55.43 ± 35.26%, mean ± SD, N = 7 larvae) and short latency (82.87 ± 5.46 ms, mean ± SD).
source: We unilaterally stimulated the population of transgenically labelled neurons in the AF7-pretectal region and observed convergent saccades paired with lateralised tail movements with high response probability (55.43 ± 35.26%, mean ± SD, N = 7 larvae) and short latency (82.87 ± 5.46 ms, mean ± SD; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: Every convergent saccade induced by population stimulation was associated with tail movement, which tended to be directed contralateral to the stimulated pretectum.
source: Every convergent saccade was associated with tail movement, which tended to be directed contralateral to the stimulated pretectum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F) similar to activation of single contra-projecting KalTA4u508 cells.
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figure

claim: No hunting-like behaviour was induced by stimulation of an off-target region or in opsin-negative animals (N = 7 larvae).
source: No hunting-like behaviour was induced by stimulation of an off-target region or in opsin-negative animals (N = 7 larvae; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Result of control experiments with reference to figure

claim: Approximately 90% of the fluorescently labelled KalTA4u508 pretectal population was typically ablated in both brain hemispheres.
source: We estimated that ~90% of the fluorescently labelled KalTA4u508 pretectal population was typically ablated in both brain hemispheres (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Result of ablation experiments with reference to figures

claim: RGC axons in AF7 were not damaged by laser ablation of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons.
source: Importantly, RGC axons in AF7 were not damaged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Result of ablation experiments with reference to figure

claim: Ablation of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons resulted in decreased hunting performance.
source: Analysis of prey consumption revealed that ablation of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons resulted in decreased hunting performance (Figure 6F).
evidence: Result of ablation experiments with reference to figure

claim: The reduction in prey-capture following ablation was associated with a reduced rate of hunting initiation as well as a reduction in the duration of hunting routines.
source: Further analysis revealed that this reduction in prey-capture was associated with a reduced rate of hunting initiation (Figure 6G) as well as a reduction in the duration of hunting routines (Figure 6H).
evidence: Result of ablation experiments with reference to figures

claim: Ablation of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons did not result in changes in average swim speeds, loom-evoked escapes or OMR performance.
source: By contrast, we did not observe changes in average swim speeds, loom-evoked escapes or OMR performance (Figure 6I–L) and control larvae did not show changes in any of the tested behaviours (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–L).
evidence: Result of ablation experiments with reference to figures

claim: Control larvae did not show changes in any of the tested behaviours following sham procedures.
source: By contrast, we did not observe changes in average swim speeds, loom-evoked escapes or OMR performance (Figure 6I–L) and control larvae did not show changes in any of the tested behaviours (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–L).
evidence: Result of control experiments with reference to figures

claim: ChR2-YFP is highly expressed in avOT in elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP larvae, as well as AF7.
source: We found that the opsin is highly expressed in avOT, as previously reported, as well as AF7 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but is absent from KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons (Figure 7D).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figures

claim: ChR2-YFP is absent from KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons in elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP larvae.
source: We found that the opsin is highly expressed in avOT, as previously reported, as well as AF7 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but is absent from KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons (Figure 7D).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figure

claim: In blind (atoh7-/-) transgenic animals, ChR2 expression was reduced in retinal arborisation fields but retained in avOT.
source: In blind (atoh7-/-) transgenic animals, ChR2 expression was reduced in retinal arborisation fields, as expected, but retained in avOT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to figure

claim: Blind elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP transgenics were more likely to display optogenetically induced hunting than their sighted siblings (29/30 responsive blind larvae vs. 13/30 sighted larvae).
source: Strikingly, we found that blind elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP transgenics were more likely to display optogenetically induced hunting than their sighted (atoh7+/+ or atoh7+/-) siblings (29/30 responsive blind larvae vs. 13/30 sighted larvae; Figure 7E–H and Video 3).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: Responsive atoh7-/- transgenics showed an increased probability of optogenetically induced hunting events, longer hunting routine durations and a substantial reduction in response latency compared to sighted siblings.
source: In addition, responsive atoh7-/- transgenics showed an increased probability of optogenetically induced hunting events, longer hunting routine durations and a substantial reduction in response latency (Figure 7I–K).
evidence: Result of optogenetic experiments with reference to figures

claim: When hunting was evoked, blind and sighted larvae showed comparable eye and tail kinematics.
source: When hunting was evoked, blind and sighted larvae showed comparable eye and tail kinematics (Figure 7L and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Kinematic comparison with reference to figures

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of avOT elicits hunting in elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP larvae.
source: These data are compatible with the conclusion of Fajardo et al. (2013), namely that optogenetic stimulation of avOT elicits hunting in elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP larvae and indicate that RGC stimulation (either visually with bright blue light, or optogenetically) interferes with induction of hunting responses.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and citation

claim: RGC stimulation (either visually with bright blue light, or optogenetically) interferes with induction of hunting responses.
source: These data are compatible with the conclusion of Fajardo et al. (2013), namely that optogenetic stimulation of avOT elicits hunting in elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP larvae and indicate that RGC stimulation (either visually with bright blue light, or optogenetically) interferes with induction of hunting responses.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Following laser-ablation of KalTA4u508 neurons, the probability of optogenetically induced hunting by avOT stimulation was substantially reduced.
source: Following laser-ablation of KalTA4u508 neurons in the same elavl3:itTA;Ptet:ChR2-YFP;KalTA4u508;UAS:mCherry larvae tested above, we observed that the probability of optogenetically induced hunting was substantially reduced (Figure 8B).
evidence: Result of ablation and optogenetic experiments with reference to figure

claim: Non-ablated control larvae showed no change in response probability to avOT stimulation between 6 and 7 dpf.
source: By contrast, non-ablated control larvae showed no change in response probability between 6 and 7 dpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: Result of control experiments with reference to figure

claim: KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons are required for release of predatory behaviour by circuits in the anterior optic tectum.
source: These data indicate that KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons are required for release of predatory behaviour by circuits in the anterior optic tectum.
evidence: Inference from ablation and optogenetic experiments

claim: KalTA4u508-expressing pretectal neurons satisfy the criteria for a command system for induction of predatory behaviour.
source: We suggest that KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons satisfy the criteria for a command system for induction of predatory behaviour.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings

claim: A command system has been defined as interneurons that are active in association with a well-defined behaviour and whose activity can induce that behaviour, but without the strict necessity requirement.
source: Thus, command systems (sometimes referred to as decision neurons, command-like neurons or higher-order neurons) have been defined as interneurons that are active in association with a well-defined behaviour and whose activity can induce that behaviour, but without the strict necessity requirement (Jing, 2009; Yoshihara and Yoshihara, 2018).
evidence: Definition from cited literature

claim: KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons are recruited during naturalistic hunting.
source: First, we showed that these cells are recruited during naturalistic hunting.
evidence: Summary of calcium imaging results

claim: KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons display no detectable activity in response to prey-like stimuli but are reliably activated when larvae release convergent saccades at the commencement of hunting.
source: We discovered that KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons, located close to AF7, display no detectable activity in response to prey-like stimuli but are reliably activated when larvae release convergent saccades at the commencement of hunting.
evidence: Summary of calcium imaging results

claim: The activity signature of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons is compatible with a premotor role in directing predatory actions, as opposed to visual encoding of prey.
source: This activity signature is compatible with a premotor role in directing predatory actions, as opposed to visual encoding of prey.
evidence: Interpretation of functional data

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of single KalTA4u508 neurons is one of the first examples of a behavioural action sequence induced by activation of a single neuron in a vertebrate.
source: As such, this is one of the first examples of a behavioural action sequence induced by activation of a single neuron in a vertebrate.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic results in context of literature

claim: Induction of hunting by single-cell optogenetic stimulation occurred in the absence of any prey-like stimulus, supporting a role for these neurons in release of predatory behaviour downstream of perceptual recognition of prey.
source: Crucially, this induction occurred in the absence of any prey-like stimulus, supporting a role for these neurons in release of predatory behaviour downstream of perceptual recognition of prey.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic results

claim: During natural behaviour, presumed downstream pattern generating circuits are unlikely to be brought to threshold by the action of single pretectal neurons.
source: These findings are compatible with the KalTA4u508 population comprising a command system controlling hunting and suggest that during natural behaviour, presumed downstream pattern generating circuits are unlikely to be brought to threshold by the action of single pretectal neurons.
evidence: Inference from comparison of single-cell vs. population optogenetic stimulation results

claim: One contributing factor to incomplete ablation effects is likely that ablations were incomplete, with 10% of labelled KalTA4u508 neurons surviving ablation.
source: One contributing factor is likely to be that ablations were incomplete. We observed that 10% of labelled KalTA4u508 neurons survived ablation and due to variegation of transgene expression (Akitake et al., 2011), this is probably a lower bound on the size of the surviving pretectal population.
evidence: Interpretation of ablation results with citation

claim: The observation that hunting can be evoked by stimulation of only a single neuron suggests few surviving cells could in principle suffice to release predatory behaviour.
source: Notably, the observation that hunting can be evoked by stimulation of only a single neuron suggests few surviving cells could in principle suffice to release predatory behaviour.
evidence: Inference from optogenetic results

claim: There might be redundant, distributed circuitry involved in hunting initiation.
source: Although hunting evoked by stimulation of anterior-ventral OT was strongly diminished in KalTA4u508-ablated animals, we do not rule out the possibility that there might be redundant, distributed circuitry involved in hunting initiation.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental results

claim: A discrete population of pretectal neurons comprises a command system controlling predatory hunting.
source: Overall, our data support the conclusion that a discrete population of pretectal neurons comprises a command system controlling predatory hunting.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental results

claim: Current evidence suggests visual recognition of prey is mediated by tectal and/or pretectal circuits.
source: Current evidence suggests visual recognition of prey is mediated by tectal and/or pretectal circuits.
evidence: Summary of literature and current findings

claim: The axon terminals of zebrafish 'projection class 2' retinal ganglion cells in AF7 appear tuned to prey-like stimuli.
source: The axon terminals of zebrafish 'projection class 2' retinal ganglion cells in AF7 appear tuned to prey-like stimuli (Semmelhack et al., 2014) and a subpopulation of tectal neurons show non-linear mixed selectivity for conjunctions of visual features that best evoke predatory responses (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Ablations of either AF7 or tectal neuropil have been shown to substantially impair hunting, compatible with an important function for these retinorecipient regions in visual perception of prey.
source: Ablations of either AF7 or tectal neuropil have been shown to substantially impair hunting (Gahtan et al., 2005; Semmelhack et al., 2014), compatible with an important function for these retinorecipient regions in visual perception of prey.
evidence: Summary of cited literature with interpretation

claim: Downstream of prey detection, the recruitment of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons might be the neural event that corresponds to the decision of the animal to initiate hunting.
source: Our data support a circuit organisation where downstream of prey detection, the recruitment of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons might be the neural event that corresponds to the decision of the animal to initiate hunting.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings

claim: The dendritic arbours of KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons lie in immediate apposition to RGC terminals in AF7, suggesting a biological interface for transforming visual sensory activity into premotor commands to release behaviour.
source: The dendritic arbours of these pretectal neurons lie in immediate apposition to RGC terminals in AF7, suggesting a biological interface for transforming visual sensory activity into premotor commands to release behaviour.
evidence: Interpretation of morphological data

claim: Photoactivation data suggests the AF7-pretectal region is closely interconnected with ipsilateral OT, providing a further route for visual prey detectors in OT to recruit a hunting response.
source: Photoactivation data also suggests the AF7-pretectal region is closely interconnected with ipsilateral OT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), providing a further route for visual prey detectors in OT to recruit a hunting response.
evidence: Interpretation of photoactivation data with reference to figure

claim: Ablation data indicate that induction of hunting by stimulation of anterior-ventral OT requires KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons.
source: Consistent with this, our ablation data indicate that induction of hunting by stimulation of anterior-ventral OT (Fajardo et al., 2013) requires KalTA4u508 pretectal neurons.
evidence: Summary of ablation results with citation

claim: The projection pattern of contralaterally projecting KalTA4u508 neurons provides a pathway for recruitment of tegmental motor pattern generators to produce the specialised eye and tail movements observed during hunting.
source: This projection pattern, as well as the identification of KalTA4u508 neurons in adult brain sections, suggests these cells reside in the larval zebrafish APN. Their axonal projections provide a pathway for recruitment of tegmental motor pattern generators to produce the specialised eye and tail movements observed during hunting (McElligott and O'malley, 2005; Bianco et al., 2011; Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of morphological data with citations

claim: It is possible that ipsilaterally projecting KalTA4u508 neurons evoke ipsilateral hunting responses by recruiting tectal efferent pathways to the ipsilateral tegmentum.
source: It is possible that this arises from recruitment of tectal efferent pathways to the ipsilateral tegmentum, which have recently been suggested to mediate prey-directed orienting turns (Helmbrecht et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation based on optogenetic results and cited literature

claim: In the presence of prey, appropriate steering signals likely derive from OT to guide lateralised orienting turns.
source: A probable explanation is that in the presence of prey, appropriate steering signals derive from OT to guide lateralised orienting turns.
evidence: Inference from comparison of optogenetic and natural hunting kinematics

claim: Compact tectal assemblies show premotor activity immediately preceding hunting initiation and are anatomically localised in relation to the directionality of hunting responses.
source: Compact tectal assemblies show premotor activity immediately preceding hunting initiation and are anatomically localised in relation to the directionality of hunting responses (Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Focal stimulation of the retinotopic tectal map has long been known to evoke goal-directed orienting responses including predatory manoeuvres.
source: Furthermore, focal stimulation of the retinotopic tectal map has long been known to evoke goal-directed orienting responses including predatory manoeuvres (Herrero et al., 1998; Bels et al., 2012) and suppression of specific populations of neurons in superior colliculus (SC) impairs visual prey detection and accurate pursuit (Hoy et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Suppression of specific populations of neurons in superior colliculus impairs visual prey detection and accurate pursuit.
source: Furthermore, focal stimulation of the retinotopic tectal map has long been known to evoke goal-directed orienting responses including predatory manoeuvres (Herrero et al., 1998; Bels et al., 2012) and suppression of specific populations of neurons in superior colliculus (SC) impairs visual prey detection and accurate pursuit (Hoy et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Pretectal activity releases predatory behaviour and operates in parallel with prey-directed steering signals, most likely from OT.
source: We hypothesise that pretectal activity releases predatory behaviour and operates in parallel with prey-directed steering signals, most likely from OT.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental findings

claim: Constant stimulation of pretectal KalTA4u508 neurons produces extended hunting sequences that commenced with saccadic eye convergence followed by serial execution of multiple swim bouts during which elevated ocular vergence was maintained.
source: Constant stimulation of pretectal KalTA4u508 neurons produces extended hunting sequences that commenced with saccadic eye convergence followed by serial execution of multiple swim bouts during which elevated ocular vergence – a hallmark of predatory behaviour – was maintained.
evidence: Summary of optogenetic results

claim: The function of pretectal activity is to induce the overall hunting programme and individual component actions are coordinated by downstream motor pattern generating circuits.
source: This suggests that the function of pretectal activity is to induce the overall hunting programme and that individual component actions (i.e. discrete tracking swim bouts) are coordinated by downstream motor pattern generating circuits.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic results

claim: In rodent studies, pathways converging on the periaqueductal grey can potently modulate predatory behaviour.
source: In recent years, several studies in rodents have demonstrated that pathways converging on the periaqueductal grey (PAG) can potently modulate predatory behaviour.
evidence: Summary of literature

claim: The central amygdala displays activity changes during hunting.
source: The central amygdala (CeA) displays activity changes during hunting (Comoli et al., 2005) and optogenetic activation of the CeA→ventral PAG pathway motivates prey pursuit (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Optogenetic activation of the CeA→ventral PAG pathway motivates prey pursuit.
source: The central amygdala (CeA) displays activity changes during hunting (Comoli et al., 2005) and optogenetic activation of the CeA→ventral PAG pathway motivates prey pursuit (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Stimulation of the medial preoptic area to vPAG pathway promotes acquisition/handling (grabbing, biting) of objects, including prey.
source: Stimulation of the medial preoptic area to vPAG pathway promotes acquisition/handling (grabbing, biting) of objects, including prey (Park et al., 2018), and activation of a GABAergic projection from lateral hypothalamus to lateral/ventrolateral PAG motivates attack on prey (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Activation of a GABAergic projection from lateral hypothalamus to lateral/ventrolateral PAG motivates attack on prey.
source: Stimulation of the medial preoptic area to vPAG pathway promotes acquisition/handling (grabbing, biting) of objects, including prey (Park et al., 2018), and activation of a GABAergic projection from lateral hypothalamus to lateral/ventrolateral PAG motivates attack on prey (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: In rodent studies where pathways to PAG were stimulated, the presence of prey, or a prey-like stimulus, was required for neuronal stimulation to induce predatory behaviour.
source: In these studies, the presence of prey, or a prey-like stimulus, was required for neuronal stimulation to induce predatory behaviour.
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Rodent pathways to PAG promote hunting by potentiating visuomotor activity, rather than directly inducing release of motor programmes downstream of sensory perception.
source: This suggests these pathways promote hunting by potentiating visuomotor activity, rather than directly inducing release of motor programmes downstream of sensory perception.
evidence: Interpretation of cited literature

claim: A glutamatergic pathway from SC to the subthalamic zona incerta responds to prey-like sensory cues and promotes hunting when optogenetically stimulated.
source: Recently, a glutamatergic pathway from SC to the subthalamic zona incerta (ZI) (Shang et al., 2019) and a GABAergic pathway from medial ZI to PAG (Zhao et al., 2019) have been shown to respond to prey-like sensory cues and promote hunting when optogenetically stimulated.
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: A GABAergic pathway from medial ZI to PAG responds to prey-like sensory cues and promotes hunting when optogenetically stimulated.
source: Recently, a glutamatergic pathway from SC to the subthalamic zona incerta (ZI) (Shang et al., 2019) and a GABAergic pathway from medial ZI to PAG (Zhao et al., 2019) have been shown to respond to prey-like sensory cues and promote hunting when optogenetically stimulated.
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of SC→ZI and ZI→PAG pathways evokes limited expression of a subset of hunting-related behaviour in the absence of prey.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation evokes limited expression of a subset of hunting-related behaviour in the absence of prey.
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: The ZI→PAG pathway appears to integrate multiple visual, vibrissal and auditory prey-related sensory signals, discriminate prey from non-prey objects, and generate a positive valence signal to motivate predation.
source: The ZI→PAG pathway appears to integrate multiple visual, vibrissal and auditory prey-related sensory signals, discriminate prey from non-prey objects, and generate a positive valence signal to motivate predation (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of cited literature

claim: Neurons that control the release of behavioural programmes represent key circuit loci at which sensory information might be integrated with internal state signals.
source: Notably, neurons that control the release of behavioural programmes, such as the KalTA4u508 pretectal cells described here, represent key circuit loci at which sensory information might be integrated with internal state signals (Flood et al., 2013).
evidence: Interpretation with citation
